strengths: Novel and clever spectral representation approach for constructing GP priors on RKHS functions, enabling closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 1) and tractable inference
Rigorous theoretical development with careful handling of measure-theoretic details (Lemmas on isonormal GPs, convergence proofs, equivalence to kernel ridge regression)
Formal analysis of prior work limitations: Propositions 1-2 rigorously characterize why BayesIMP's nuclear-dominant kernels lead to systematic underfitting and variance collapse
Comprehensive empirical validation across toy, synthetic, and healthcare benchmarks demonstrating consistent improvements; ablation studies quantifying contributions of calibration tuning
Principled calibration algorithm (Algorithm 2) to tune spectral measure for optimal coverage, addressing a real concern about posterior miscalibration
Clear presentation of method's advantages: avoids dense estimation, propensity weighting, and arbitrary bespoke kernels; maintains equivalence to established Singh et al. (2024) point estimator
weaknesses: Critical concern with modeling assumptions: Eqs. (10)-(11) are explicitly characterized as 'purely probabilistic surrogates' rather than structural models, undermining causal interpretation and posterior reliability under misspecification; no formal analysis of robustness to assumption violations

Artificial observation model for spectral coordinates: Eq. (11) assumes direct noisy observations of ϕ_{V,i}(V), which are not observable; unclear how these are obtained in causal data fusion settings (Sec. A.4)

Spectral measure selection lacks principled guidance: ν is a free parameter, Algorithm 2 tunes it via grid search over β, but sensitivity analysis is missing and default choice yields poor calibration (Table 4: error drops from 0.087 to 0.065 with tuning)
Weaker theoretical guarantees than frequentist alternatives: no convergence rates for posterior means/quantiles, no asymptotic calibration conditions, analysis limited to well-specified regime only

Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: O(n³) complexity not tested for n > 1000; computing K̃_V via Monte Carlo introduces O_p(m^{-1/2}) error; Algorithm 2 (calibration) is computationally expensive with unclear practical guidance

Experimental limitations: small sample sizes (n=100-500) with unclear robustness to scaling; healthcare example uses simulator rather than real data; modest improvements in some metrics (RMSE differences often overlap in error bars)

Incomplete presentation: Assumption 3 (Mercer conditions) critical but relegated to appendix; function class expansion (Sec. 3.1) not well motivated philosophically; GP credible interval approximation (Sec. 4.2) lacks error analysis; no comparison to debiased machine learning or detailed computational cost analysis

strengths: Clever spectral decomposition approach using Mercer's theorem to handle vector-valued RKHS functions, enabling tractable GP inference
Clear and rigorous identification of BayesIMP pathologies (nonstationarity, variance collapse) with formal analysis in Section A.6
Closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 1) providing exact inference without approximation for posterior mean and variance
Posterior means theoretically match Singh et al. (2024) KRR estimators, establishing principled uncertainty quantification
Comprehensive mathematical development with rigorous proofs and extensions (causal data fusion, incremental effects)
weaknesses: Critical modeling assumptions (Eqs. 10-11) acknowledged as 'probabilistic surrogates' rather than structural models, undermining soundness of posterior inferences without clear justification of when reasonable
Free spectral measure parameter ν with ad-hoc calibration via Algorithm 2 requiring expensive bootstrap; no theoretical guidance on grid choice or convergence
KL-divergence GP approximation (Section 4.2) lacks rigor: KL divergence between stochastic processes defined informally, no bounds on approximation quality or coverage properties

Weak experimental validation: only synthetic/simulated data with modest improvements (~30% RMSE on toy problem), no real-world causal inference validation, no comparison to recent Bayesian/causal ML methods
Scalability not addressed: computational cost of sampling from ν to compute K̃_V (claimed O(m) with m >> 10⁶) not analyzed, all experiments on small datasets (n ≤ 500)
Narrow scope: only applicable to Singh et al. (2024) RKHS framework with continuous treatments; unclear generalizability
Insufficient practical guidance: kernel selection procedures, sensitivity analyses, and violation consequences not discussed
Missing finite-sample theoretical guarantees: no coverage probabilities for credible intervals, no convergence rates for spectral truncation

strengths: Novel spectral representation approach for GP priors on RKHS functions—elegant solution to fundamental challenges in prior work
Closed-form posterior moments for causal effects (Theorem 1), achieving exact Bayesian inference for a non-trivial problem
Rigorous analysis of BayesIMP limitations (Propositions 1-2): underfitting from kernel non-stationarity and variance collapse out-of-distribution
Posterior mean recovers kernel ridge regression estimator (Singh et al. 2024), establishing equivalence with state-of-the-art point estimator
Comprehensive experiments with consistent improvements in RMSE and calibration across toy example, synthetic benchmarks, and causal Bayesian optimization
Well-written with transparent treatment of modeling assumptions, extensive proofs, and helpful analysis of prior work
weaknesses: Restrictive observation models (Eqs. 10-11) treat true conditional expectations as noisy observations—'probabilistic surrogates' rather than structural assumptions, limiting generality
Limited theoretical analysis: no convergence rates, no finite-sample coverage guarantees for credible intervals, and heuristic KL-optimal GP approximation not validated
Empirical improvements are modest and often within confidence interval overlap (e.g., Table 2: RMSE 0.361±0.158 vs 0.378±0.126 for BayesIMP)
Spectral measure selection via grid search (Algorithm 2) is not fully principled; arbitrary parametrization νβ=N(V̄,β²I) lacks justification
No comparison to simpler baselines: doubly-robust methods with bootstrap, frequentist confidence intervals on Singh et al. (2024) estimator, or direct bootstrap uncertainty quantification
Healthcare validation uses simulator rather than real observational/interventional data, limiting confidence in practical utility
Limited scope: continuous treatments only, requires causal graph specification, all experiments small sample size (n≤500) with O(n³) complexity

strengths: Novel and elegant solution to placing GP priors on RKHS functions via spectral representations, enabling tractable inference for causal uncertainty quantification
Comprehensive theoretical analysis including closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 4.1), recovery of kernel ridge regression estimator, and approximation error bounds (Section A.4)
Detailed mathematical characterization of BayesIMP limitations (Propositions A.10-A.11) with convincing empirical demonstration of underfitting and variance collapse
Thorough experimental validation across synthetic benchmarks, causal Bayesian optimization, and real dataset, with appropriate baselines and proper statistical confidence intervals
Clear presentation of practical algorithms (hyperparameter tuning via closed-form objective, calibration procedure) with transparent discussion of surrogate likelihood approximations
Well-organized paper with comprehensive appendix providing proofs, additional experiments, and robustness checks (Tables 5-8)
weaknesses: Multiple stacked approximations (surrogate likelihood for Eq. 11, Gaussian moment-matching for intervals, MC approximation of K̃_V, spectral truncation) whose joint finite-sample impact on coverage is not formally characterized, limiting confidence in reliability

Limited finite-sample theoretical guarantees: no asymptotic normality or coverage results for the posterior, calibration consistency (Theorem C.9) requires sample-splitting and smoothness conditions whose verification is unclear

Spectral eigendecomposition (λ_{V,i}, φ_{V,i}) remains unknown in practice; implementation via MC approximation of K̃_V introduces another error layer with vague guidance on choosing number of samples m
Credible intervals rely on Gaussian moment-matching projection that may perform poorly when true posterior deviates from Gaussian, with no empirical quantification of approximation impact on coverage

Calibration procedure itself is approximate and tuning-intensive: grid search over β ∈ {2^{-4,-2,0,2,4}} appears ad-hoc, requires bootstrap replications, and uses plug-in estimator γ̂ introducing additional bias
Computational scalability concerns: O(n³) complexity from matrix inversions, minibatch SGD only for training not inference, limits application to very large datasets
Experimental scale limited to n=100 in synthetic benchmarks; 401(k) dataset lacks ground truth; limited robustness investigation beyond one kernel ablation (Table 7)

strengths: Novel use of spectral representations to enable tractable GP priors for RKHS-valued functions while avoiding pathologies of previous approaches
Closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 4.1) with provable equivalence to Singh et al. (2024) kernel estimator
Rigorous theoretical development including convergence analysis (L² properties) and likelihood misspecification bounds
Thorough characterization of BayesIMP limitations (Section A.6) with mathematical proofs of underfitting and variance collapse
Practical calibration procedure with consistency guarantees and grid-search implementation
Comprehensive experiments across synthetic benchmarks and Bayesian optimization tasks showing improvements over BayesIMP
weaknesses: Critical reliance on surrogate Gaussian likelihoods (Eq. 11) that are not the true data-generating process with limited empirical validation that approximation holds on real data
Posterior coverage guarantees depend on surrogate likelihood being reasonable, but error bounds require likelihood ratio moment control that is difficult to verify in practice
Calibration algorithm requires ground-truth causal estimates at many points and is post-hoc; cannot validate coverage on real 401(k) data where ground truth is unavailable
Unfair baseline comparison: main competitor BayesIMP had implementation bugs (typos) that authors had to fix, making comparison less convincing
Missing comparison with frequentist methods (Kennedy et al., Oprescu et al.) in main experiments; only included in limited synthetic benchmarks
Very dense presentation with heavy notation; key insights about function class expansion and avoiding pathologies buried in technical details
Limited practical guidance on choosing spectral measure family in calibration and sensitivity to this choice
Momentum-matching GP approximation (Eq. 20) for credible intervals introduces error not quantified; unknown how much coverage is lost
Computational requirements unclear for large datasets; 401(k) uses non-standard minibatch SGD for GP hyperparameter training
Multiple hyperparameters require tuning (kernels, lengthscales, noise variances, spectral measure) with limited guidance provided

strengths: Novel spectral representation approach elegantly avoids pathologies of prior RKHS GP constructions by expanding function classes, enabling standard GP machinery while ensuring posterior mean recovery of the original kernel estimator
Closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 4.1) with tractable computation and novel weighted likelihood objective (Eq. 22) for hyperparameter tuning, contrasting favorably with intractable alternatives
Principled calibration algorithm (Algorithm 2) via spectral measure learning that achieves frequentist coverage guarantees with consistency proof (Theorem C.9)

Comprehensive experimental validation: toy example demonstrating clear advantages over BayesIMP, synthetic benchmark with in/out-of-distribution evaluation, causal BO applications, and 401(k) real-world case study
Rigorous mathematical development with clear assumptions (A.1-A.4), detailed proofs of L² convergence and posterior properties, thorough treatment of isonormal GPs and spectral theory
Thorough and fair analysis of related work limitations, particularly Propositions A.10-A.11 characterizing BayesIMP kernel non-stationarity and variance collapse pathologies
Honest discussion of limitations: surrogate likelihood approximations, moment-matched Gaussian approximation scope, and suggestions for future work on richer posterior approximations
weaknesses: Surrogate likelihood model (Eq. 11) assumes coordinate-wise additive Gaussian noise on spectral features; validity boundaries unclear with only limited sensitivity analysis (Section A.4) not fully validating when approximations hold

Moment-matched Gaussian approximation (Eq. 20) for credible intervals introduces bias; calibration only adjusts spectral measure scale β but cannot fix distributional mismatch for truly non-Gaussian posteriors

Spectral measure selection crucial but somewhat arbitrary; paper proposes ν = N(V̄, β²I) with limited justification; calibration only tunes scale parameter, not family choice, providing limited guidance to practitioners

Dense presentation with heavy notation and complex expressions (e.g., Theorem 4.1) potentially limiting accessibility; spectral machinery and Mercer expansions may be inaccessible to applied practitioners

Scalability limited by O(n³) matrix operations; posterior inference requires full data despite minibatch SGD for hyperparameter training; 401(k) experiment (n≈10,000) moderate-sized, unclear performance for larger datasets

Limited scope of comparison: only BayesIMP specifically designed for this setting; comparisons to ORF and Continuous DR are indirect since they don't directly output functional uncertainty; missing comparisons to bootstrap, frequentist asymptotics, or other Bayesian non-parametric approaches
Theoretical calibration results show estimator consistency (Theorem C.9) but not finite-sample coverage guarantees after calibration; grid-search approach practical but not optimality-guaranteed
Missing identifiability robustness analysis: assumes backdoor/front-door criteria without sensitivity study; no simulation experiments exploring effects of unmeasured confounding
